items.q: What is the sum of the series <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n</annotation></semantics></math>?

mistakes.why: That is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_1 = a_1</annotation></semantics></math>, the first partial sum. The sum is where the partial sums head as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> grows.

That is the limit of the terms <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_n</annotation></semantics></math>. The sum of the series is the limit of the partial sums <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_n</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Find <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_3</annotation></semantics></math>, the third term of the series.

mistakes.why: That is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_3</annotation></semantics></math>, the sum of the first three terms. The third term alone is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_3 - S_2</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Write the general term <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_n</annotation></semantics></math> of the series in terms of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: That is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_n</annotation></semantics></math>, the sum of the first <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> terms. The <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>th term is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_n - S_{n-1}</annotation></semantics></math>.

Subtract the whole previous partial sum: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_n</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{3n}{n + 2} - \frac{3(n - 1)}{n + 1}</annotation></semantics></math>, over a common denominator.

items.q: Which statement about this series is correct?
options: The terms converge to 3, so the series converges

The series diverges, since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_n</annotation></semantics></math> keeps growing as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> grows
The series converges to 3, and its terms approach 0
The series converges to 3, and its terms approach 3

items.q: Find <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=5}^{\infty} a_n</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: That is the sum from <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n = 1</annotation></semantics></math>. Starting at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n = 5</annotation></semantics></math> leaves out <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + a_4</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= S_4</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 2</annotation></semantics></math>.

That subtracts <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>15</mn><mn>7</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_5 = \frac{15}{7}</annotation></semantics></math>, which includes <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_5</annotation></semantics></math>. Subtract only the terms before <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n = 5</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_4</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Find <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>100</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{100}</annotation></semantics></math>, the sum of the first 100 terms.

mistakes.why: Odd partial sums are 1; with an even number of terms, every 1 is canceled by a <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math>.

The terms are not all 1: they alternate between 1 and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Does the series <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (-1)^{n+1}</annotation></semantics></math> converge?
options: Yes, to 0, since the even partial sums are 0
Yes, to 1, since the first term is 1

Yes, since each term is 1 or <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> and so stays bounded
No: the partial sums jump between 1 and 0

items.q: A student writes <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>⋯</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1 - 1) + (1 - 1) + \cdots</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 0</annotation></semantics></math>, and then <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>⋯</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1 + (-1 + 1) + (-1 + 1) + \cdots</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 1</annotation></semantics></math>. What is the flaw?
options: The first grouping is right, so the sum is 0
The second grouping is right, so the sum is 1
Regrouping the terms changes the partial sums; the series has no sum

Both are right, so the sum is the average, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>

items.q: A student says the sum of this series is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, the average of the values of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_n</annotation></semantics></math>. Is that correct?
options: Yes: the partial sums center on <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>
No: the series diverges, so it has no sum
No: the sum is 0, from the even partial sums
No: the sum is 1, the first partial sum

items.q: Find the sum <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{2}{n(n + 2)}</annotation></semantics></math>. (Hint: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{2}{n(n + 2)}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{n + 2}</annotation></semantics></math>.)

mistakes.why: Two positive pieces survive the canceling, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, because each term cancels with the one two places later.

That is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_1 = 1 - \frac{1}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>. The sum is the limit of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_n</annotation></semantics></math> as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n \to \infty</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: The partial sums of a series are <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_n = \frac{n^2}{n^2 + 1}</annotation></semantics></math>. Find the fourth term, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_4</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: That is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_4</annotation></semantics></math>, the sum of the first four terms. Subtract <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_3</annotation></semantics></math> to get the fourth term alone.

That is the sum of the series, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim S_n</annotation></semantics></math>, not a single term.

items.q: The partial sums of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \ln\left(\frac{n + 1}{n}\right)</annotation></semantics></math> are <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_n = \ln(n + 1)</annotation></semantics></math>. What does this show?
options: The series converges, since its terms approach 0

The series converges to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln 2</annotation></semantics></math>, its first term
The series diverges, though its terms approach 0
The series converges to 0

items.q: For a series <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n</annotation></semantics></math>, what is the partial sum <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_n</annotation></semantics></math>?
options: The <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>th term, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_n</annotation></semantics></math>

The sum of the first <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> terms, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>⋯</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n</annotation></semantics></math>
The sum of the terms after the <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>th one

The limit of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_n</annotation></semantics></math> as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n \to \infty</annotation></semantics></math>

items.q: The partial sums of a series are <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_n = 5 - \frac{2}{n}</annotation></semantics></math>. Find the first term, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_1</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: That is the sum of the series, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{n \to \infty} S_n</annotation></semantics></math>. The first term is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_1</annotation></semantics></math>.

2 is the amount subtracted at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n = 1</annotation></semantics></math>, not the term. The first term is the first partial sum: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>1</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_1 = S_1 = 5 - \frac{2}{1} = 3</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 4</annotation></semantics></math>. Find <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 3a_n</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: Multiplying every term by 3 multiplies every partial sum, and so the sum, by 3.
A constant factor multiplies the sum; it is not added to it.

items.q: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum a_n</annotation></semantics></math> converges and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum b_n</annotation></semantics></math> diverges. What can be said about <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum (a_n + b_n)</annotation></semantics></math>?
options: It converges
It may converge or diverge
It diverges

It converges to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum a_n</annotation></semantics></math>

items.q: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n</annotation></semantics></math> converges to 10, and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>⋯</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>99</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_{99} = 7</annotation></semantics></math>. What is true of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=100}^{\infty} a_n</annotation></semantics></math>?
options: It converges, to 10
It converges, to 3
It diverges: an infinite tail has no sum
It converges, to 7

items.q: Find the common ratio <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: That divides a term by the one after it. The ratio is a term over the previous term: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mn>12</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{-8}{12}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The signs alternate, so the ratio is negative.

items.q: Does the series converge?
options: No: the terms alternate in sign
No: the first term, 12, is greater than 1

Yes: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo><</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|r| = \frac{2}{3} < 1</annotation></semantics></math>

Yes: the ratio <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\frac{2}{3}</annotation></semantics></math> is negative

items.q: Find <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: The ratio is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\frac{2}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1 - r = 1 + \frac{2}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>. Using <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1 - \frac{2}{3}</annotation></semantics></math> drops the sign.

That divides the ratio's term <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-8</annotation></semantics></math> by <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1 - r</annotation></semantics></math>. The numerator is the first term, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a = 12</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Find <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} a_n</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: That uses 12 as the first term. The first term of the sum from <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n = 2</annotation></semantics></math> is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>16</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_2 = \frac{16}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>.

That removes only <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_0 = 12</annotation></semantics></math>. Starting at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n = 2</annotation></semantics></math> removes <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_1</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>36</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{36}{5} - 12 - (-8)</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Find <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_3 = a_0 + a_1 + a_2</annotation></semantics></math>, the sum of the first three terms.

mistakes.why: That is the sum of all the terms. <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_3</annotation></semantics></math> adds the first three only.

That adds <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_0</annotation></semantics></math> through <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_3</annotation></semantics></math>, four terms; <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_3</annotation></semantics></math> stops at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_2</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: What is the common ratio of this series?
options: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x - 1</annotation></semantics></math>
<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{x - 1}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{3}{x - 1}</annotation></semantics></math>

items.q: Give all <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> for which the series converges, as an interval.

ends.lo: At <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = -2</annotation></semantics></math> the ratio is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math>: the terms are <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(-1)^n</annotation></semantics></math>, whose partial sums jump between 1 and 0, so the series diverges and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = -2</annotation></semantics></math> is left out.
ends.hi: At <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = 4</annotation></semantics></math> the ratio is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>: every term is 1 and the partial sums grow without bound, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = 4</annotation></semantics></math> is left out.

mistakes.why: At <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = -2</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = 4</annotation></semantics></math> the ratio has size 1, and a geometric series with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|r| = 1</annotation></semantics></math> diverges. Leave both ends out.

That interval is centered at 0. Here <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo><</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|x - 1| < 3</annotation></semantics></math> is centered at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = 1</annotation></semantics></math>: from <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1 - 3</annotation></semantics></math> to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1 + 3</annotation></semantics></math>.

At <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = 4</annotation></semantics></math> the ratio is 1, so every term is 1 and the series diverges.

interval.answerHtml: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(-2, 4)</annotation></semantics></math>

items.q: For <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-2 < x < 4</annotation></semantics></math>, write the sum of the series as an expression in <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3 - (x - 1)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 3 - x + 1</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 4 - x</annotation></semantics></math>: the minus sign reaches the <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> too.

The ratio is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{x - 1}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>, not <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>: the sum is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{1 - \frac{x - 1}{3}}</annotation></semantics></math>.

The series starts at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n = 0</annotation></semantics></math> with the term 1, so that term stays in the sum.

items.q: For which <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> is the sum of the series equal to 2?

mistakes.why: Check the algebra: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4 - x = \frac{3}{2}</annotation></semantics></math> gives <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = 4 - \frac{3}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. Also <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>11</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{11}{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is outside the interval where the series converges.

items.q: Write the repeating decimal <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.272727</mn><mo>…</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.272727\ldots</annotation></semantics></math> as a fraction in lowest terms.

mistakes.why: That is the first term only. The sum is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{a}{1 - r}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>100</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = \frac{1}{100}</annotation></semantics></math>.

Each repeat shifts two places, so the ratio is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>100</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{100}</annotation></semantics></math>, not <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>10</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{10}</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>27</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{27/100}{1 - 1/10}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>10</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{3}{10}</annotation></semantics></math> uses the wrong ratio.

items.q: Find <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mn>5</mn><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 5\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^n</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: That uses 5 as the first term, the value at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n = 0</annotation></semantics></math>. This sum starts at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n = 1</annotation></semantics></math>, where the term is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>5</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{5}{4}</annotation></semantics></math>.

That is the first term only; divide by <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1 - r = \frac{3}{4}</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Find <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mfrac><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{2^n}{3^{n+1}}</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: That treats the first term as 1. At <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n = 0</annotation></semantics></math> the term is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>0</mn></msup><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>1</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{2^0}{3^1} = \frac{1}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>.

Rewrite the term as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n</annotation></semantics></math>; the sum is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1/3}{1 - 2/3}</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Does <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mfrac><msup><mn>3</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{3^n}{2^n}</annotation></semantics></math> converge?
options: Yes: to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{1 - 3/2} = -2</annotation></semantics></math>
Yes: it is geometric
No: its ratio <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{2}{3}</annotation></semantics></math> is less than 1

No: it is geometric with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = \frac{3}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|r| \ge 1</annotation></semantics></math>

items.q: A ball is dropped from 10 feet. After each bounce it rises to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{3}{4}</annotation></semantics></math> of the height it fell from. Find the total vertical distance it travels, up and down, if it bounces forever.

mistakes.why: That counts each rebound height once. The ball goes up and then comes back down the same height.
The first 10 feet is traveled once (down only); only the rebound heights are traveled twice.

items.q: For which values of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> does <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} r^n</annotation></semantics></math> converge? Give an interval.

ends.lo: At <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = -1</annotation></semantics></math> the partial sums jump between 1 and 0, so the series diverges.
ends.hi: At <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = 1</annotation></semantics></math> every term is 1 and the partial sums grow without bound, so the series diverges.

mistakes.why: At <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = 1</annotation></semantics></math> the series is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mo>⋯</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1 + 1 + \cdots</annotation></semantics></math> and at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = -1</annotation></semantics></math> it is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mo>⋯</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1 - 1 + 1 - \cdots</annotation></semantics></math>: both diverge.

At <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = 1</annotation></semantics></math> every term is 1, and the partial sums <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_n = n</annotation></semantics></math> grow without bound.

interval.answerHtml: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(-1, 1)</annotation></semantics></math>

items.q: Find <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} e^{-n}</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: That is the sum from <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n = 0</annotation></semantics></math>, which includes the term <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^0 = 1</annotation></semantics></math>. Here the first term is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math>.

That is the first term only; divide by <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>e</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1 - r = 1 - \frac{1}{e}</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: For <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r \ne 1</annotation></semantics></math>, what is the sum of the first <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> terms of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mo>⋯</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a + ar + ar^2 + \cdots</annotation></semantics></math>?
options: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{a}{1 - r}</annotation></semantics></math>

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a\,r^{n}</annotation></semantics></math>

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{a(1 - r^{n+1})}{1 - r}</annotation></semantics></math>

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{a(1 - r^n)}{1 - r}</annotation></semantics></math>

items.q: Find <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: The terms in the table head toward 2, not 0: the top and bottom have the same degree.

That divides the top's coefficient 2 by the bottom's constant 5. For large <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> the leading terms <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2n^2</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n^2</annotation></semantics></math> decide the limit.

items.q: What does the nth term test say about <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum a_n</annotation></semantics></math>?
options: It converges to 2, since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim a_n = 2</annotation></semantics></math>
Nothing, since the terms approach a limit
It converges, since the terms level off

It diverges, since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim a_n = 2 \ne 0</annotation></semantics></math>

items.q: What does the nth term test say about <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum b_n</annotation></semantics></math>?
options: It converges, since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim b_n = 0</annotation></semantics></math>
It diverges, since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_n</annotation></semantics></math> is positive

Nothing: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim b_n = 0</annotation></semantics></math>
It diverges, since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1000</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{1000}</annotation></semantics></math> is not 0

items.q: What does the nth term test say about <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum c_n</annotation></semantics></math>?
options: Nothing, since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{n} \to 0</annotation></semantics></math>

It diverges, since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim c_n = \cos 0 = 1 \ne 0</annotation></semantics></math>

It converges, since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)</annotation></semantics></math> stays bounded
It converges to 1

items.q: Find <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: The dots rise toward the dashed line at 3; they do not approach 0.

That is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_1</annotation></semantics></math>, the first term. The limit is where the terms head as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> grows: divide the top and bottom by <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Which conclusion about <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n</annotation></semantics></math> is correct?
options: The series converges to 3
The nth term test is inconclusive
The series converges, since each <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_n</annotation></semantics></math> is below 3
The series diverges by the nth term test

items.q: How do the partial sums <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_n</annotation></semantics></math> behave for large <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>?
options: They approach 3, the limit of the terms
They approach 0
They grow without bound
They level off at some number greater than 3

items.q: A student writes: \"The terms converge to 3, so the series converges to 3.\" What is wrong?
options: Nothing: a series converges to the limit of its terms
A limit of 3 for the terms makes the series diverge
The terms converge to 0, not 3
The series converges, but to a number other than 3

items.q: Which statement is the nth term test?
options: If <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n \ne 0</annotation></semantics></math>, then <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum a_n</annotation></semantics></math> diverges

If <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0</annotation></semantics></math>, then <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum a_n</annotation></semantics></math> converges

If <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum a_n</annotation></semantics></math> diverges, then <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n \ne 0</annotation></semantics></math>

If <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0</annotation></semantics></math>, then <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum a_n</annotation></semantics></math> diverges

items.q: What does the nth term test say about <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mi>arctan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \arctan n</annotation></semantics></math>?
options: It converges: arctan is bounded by <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\pi}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>

Nothing: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arctan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arctan n</annotation></semantics></math> is increasing, not decreasing
It converges to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\pi}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>

It diverges: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mi>arctan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim \arctan n = \frac{\pi}{2} \ne 0</annotation></semantics></math>

items.q: What does the nth term test say about <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mfrac><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n^2}{e^n}</annotation></semantics></math>?
options: It diverges: the top and bottom both grow
It converges: the terms approach 0
Nothing: the terms approach 0

It diverges: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{n^2}{e^n}</annotation></semantics></math> is positive

items.q: What does the nth term test say about <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>n</mi></msup><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n\,n}{n + 1}</annotation></semantics></math>?
options: Nothing: the terms alternate in sign
It diverges: the terms do not approach 0
It converges: positive and negative terms cancel

Nothing: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim a_n</annotation></semantics></math> does not exist

items.q: For which constant <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is the nth term test inconclusive for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{kn + 1}{2n + 3}</annotation></semantics></math>?

mistakes.why: For <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k = 2</annotation></semantics></math> the terms approach <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{2}{2} = 1 \ne 0</annotation></semantics></math>, so the test shows divergence.

That makes the first term 0 (<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k + 1 = 0</annotation></semantics></math>), but the test is about the limit as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n \to \infty</annotation></semantics></math>, which is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{k}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Which justification earns credit for the divergence of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{4n - 1}{n + 2}</annotation></semantics></math>?
options: The terms converge to 4, so the series converges to 4
The terms get bigger, so the series diverges

The series diverges because <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{4n - 1}{n + 2}</annotation></semantics></math> diverges

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{4n - 1}{n + 2}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 4 \ne 0</annotation></semantics></math>; it diverges by the nth term test

items.q: Find <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><mi>n</mi><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{n \to \infty} n\sin\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, the limit of the terms of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mi>n</mi><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n\sin\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) \to 0</annotation></semantics></math>, but it is multiplied by <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n \to \infty</annotation></semantics></math>. Rewrite as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow><mi>u</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\sin u}{u}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u = \frac{1}{n}</annotation></semantics></math>.

Use the limit, not a large <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>. The two factors balance: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow><mi>u</mi></mfrac><mo>→</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\sin u}{u} \to 1</annotation></semantics></math> as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u \to 0</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: What can be concluded about <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n + 1}</annotation></semantics></math> from the nth term test alone?
options: It converges, since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{n + 1} \to 0</annotation></semantics></math>
Nothing: the terms approach 0

It diverges, since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{n + 1} \to 0</annotation></semantics></math>
It converges to 0

items.q: What does the integral test say about <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2 + 1}</annotation></semantics></math>?
options: It converges, since its integral is finite
It converges to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\pi}{4}</annotation></semantics></math>
It diverges, since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\pi}{4}</annotation></semantics></math> is not 0
Nothing, since the integral is not a whole number

items.q: A student concludes from the table that <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 1</annotation></semantics></math>. Is that right?
options: Yes: the integral test gives the sum
No: the series diverges, though the integral is finite

Yes: both are limits of sums of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{x^2}</annotation></semantics></math>
No: the integral decides convergence but is not the sum

items.q: What does the integral test say about <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n\ln n}</annotation></semantics></math>?
options: It converges, since its terms approach 0
Nothing, since the series starts at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n = 2</annotation></semantics></math>
It diverges, since its integral diverges

It converges, since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\ln n</annotation></semantics></math> grows faster than <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>

items.q: Verify the table's value: find <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mn>1</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_1^{\infty} \frac{dx}{x^2 + 1}</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: That is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><mi>arctan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{b \to \infty} \arctan b</annotation></semantics></math> alone. Subtract <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arctan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arctan 1 = \frac{\pi}{4}</annotation></semantics></math> for the lower limit.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arctan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arctan 1 = \frac{\pi}{4}</annotation></semantics></math> is subtracted, not added.

items.q: To use the integral test on <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mfrac><mi>n</mi><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n}{n^2 + 1}</annotation></semantics></math>, which must be checked about <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>x</mi><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x) = \frac{x}{x^2 + 1}</annotation></semantics></math>, and does it hold?
options: That <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is decreasing for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x \ge 1</annotation></semantics></math>: yes, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≤</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(x) \le 0</annotation></semantics></math> there

That <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is increasing for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x \ge 1</annotation></semantics></math>: yes, since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> grows

That <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(n)</annotation></semantics></math> approaches 0: yes, so the series converges

That <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is decreasing for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x \ge 0</annotation></semantics></math>: no, so the test fails

items.q: On which interval is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> decreasing?
options: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x \ge 0</annotation></semantics></math>
<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x \le 1</annotation></semantics></math>
<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x \ge e</annotation></semantics></math>
<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x \ge 1</annotation></semantics></math>

items.q: Find <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int xe^{-x}\,dx</annotation></semantics></math> (integration by parts).

mistakes.why: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int e^{-x}\,dx = -e^{-x}</annotation></semantics></math>, so the second term is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-e^{-x}</annotation></semantics></math>.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \int e^{-x}\,dx</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= -e^{-x}</annotation></semantics></math>; the <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">uv</annotation></semantics></math> term is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-xe^{-x}</annotation></semantics></math>.

The integral of a product is not the product of integrals: use parts with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u = x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">dv = e^{-x}\,dx</annotation></semantics></math>.
